subtitle: "Baseline characteristics of your study population with gtsummary"

description: "Build a Table 1 of baseline characteristics with gtsummary in R, add a crude incidence rate per 1000 person-years, and export it to Excel, Word or CSV."

A **Table 1** describes your study population: age, sex and other baseline
variables, usually split by exposure. It is almost always the first table in a
register-based paper. This page builds one from the analysis-ready dataset with
the [`gtsummary`](https://www.danieldsjoberg.com/gtsummary/) package, adds a
crude incidence rate per group, and writes the table to a file you can take
through output control.

*Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own.*
`gtsummary` - and `huxtable`, if you want to export to Excel - must be installed
in your R environment on DST (Statistics Denmark); if they are not, contact your data manager.

## Starting point

You start from your analysis-ready dataset with one row per person ([Phase
12](data-manipulation.qmd)), or one row per person and index date if your
comparison group was matched with replacement.

```r
library(dplyr) # %>% (pipe)
library(gtsummary) # tbl_summary() + export functions

df <- readRDS("path/to/analysis.rds") # analysis-ready dataset, one row per person (per person and index date if matched with replacement)
```

## Build the table with `tbl_summary()` {#example}

`tbl_summary()` summarises the variables you point it at. With `by =` you split
the table into columns by a group (e.g. exposure).

```r
table1 <- df %>%
  tbl_summary(
    by = exposure, # one column per group (omit for an overall table)
    include = c(age, sex, nmi), # variables to include
    statistic = list(
      all_continuous() ~ "{median} ({p25}, {p75})",
      all_categorical() ~ "{n} ({p}%)"
    ),
    digits = all_continuous() ~ 1, # number of decimals for continuous numbers
    label = list(age ~ "Age (years)", sex ~ "Sex", nmi ~ "NMI score"), # nice variable names
    missing = "ifany", # show an "unknown" row if values are missing
    missing_text = "Missing" # the text for that row
  ) %>%
  add_overall() %>% # add an "Overall" column: ALL participants combined (both groups)
  bold_labels() %>% # bold the variable names
  modify_header(label ~ "**Variable**") # text in the header of the variable column (your choice)

table1 # print the table (display it)
```

<details>
<summary>How `tbl_summary()` picks the statistics, and what each argument does</summary>

- **`tbl_summary()` detects the variable type itself** from the column's contents and picks a suitable statistic:
  - factor and character variables - and numeric variables with **fewer than 10 unique values** - become *categorical* and are shown as `{n} ({p}%)` (count and percentage);
  - other numeric variables become *continuous* and are shown as `{median} ({p25}, {p75})` (median and quartiles, i.e. interquartile range, IQR);
  - variables coded `0/1`, `yes/no` or `TRUE/FALSE` become *dichotomous* and are shown with only the one ("yes") row.
- **`statistic =` is therefore optional.** Omit the line entirely and you get exactly the default display above. It is only included to show how you *change* it - for mean instead of median, write `all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})"`.
- In `gtsummary` the tilde `~` means "assign": `what ~ value`. E.g. `age ~ "Age (years)"` gives the `age` variable the label "Age (years)", and `all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})"` sets that statistic for all continuous variables.
- `all_continuous()` / `all_categorical()` mean "all continuous" resp. "all categorical" variables, so the rule applies to all of them at once.
- `digits` controls the number of decimals (here 1 for the continuous variables).
- `add_overall()` adds an **Overall column** with all participants combined (both groups in one column), next to the per-group columns - handy for showing the total count and overall distribution. Omit it if you only want the groups.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Should you add p-values?</summary>

You can add a p-value column with `add_p()`. You can either run it **afterwards** on the finished `table1` (as here), or insert `add_p()` into the chain above right after `tbl_summary()` - the result is the same. Note that hypothesis tests in a plain baseline table are often discouraged (with large register populations they do not test what people assume). Use them deliberately.

```r
table1 %>%           # take the already-built table ...
  add_p()            # ... and add a column of p-values
```

</details>

## Crude incidence rate (per 1000 person-years) {#crude-rate}

Register papers often report the crude incidence rate per exposure group
alongside Table 1: the number of events divided by the total follow-up time
(person-years), scaled to per 1000 person-years. It needs `outcome` (1 = event, 0 =
censored) and `followup_years` from your analysis-ready dataset (built in [Phase
12](joins.qmd#follow-up-time)).

```r
df %>%
  group_by(exposure) %>% # one line per exposure group
  summarise(
    events = sum(outcome), # number of outcomes in the group
    person_years = sum(followup_years), # total follow-up time (person-years)
    rate_per_1000 = sum(outcome) / sum(followup_years) * 1000 # crude rate per 1000 person-years
  )
```

For a 95% confidence interval around one group's rate, put that group's events
and person-years into `poisson.test()` (base R, exact Poisson interval):

```r
poisson.test(x = 37, T = 4210)$conf.int * 1000 # 37 events, 4210 person-years -> CI per 1000 person-years
```

This is a descriptive rate with no adjustment. The number of events is a cell
like any other, so check it against the small-cell rule before export. To
compare the groups with control for confounding, see [Rates and rate ratios
(Poisson)](rates-poisson.qmd) for an adjusted rate ratio or
[Time-to-event](time-to-event.qmd), where a Cox model gives a hazard ratio.

## Export the table (for output control)

Anything leaving DST must go through output control, and the rules are on
[Phase 14 - Export and repatriation](export.qmd). Before you write the file,
check three things in the table:

- **Small cells.** Every count, including the "Missing" row, must be at or
  above your project's threshold (3 or 5).
- **Hidden numbers.** If you hide a count, the Overall column and the N in the
  header can give it back. See [a hidden number must not be possible to work
  out](export.qmd#back-calculation).
- **Median and quartiles.** DST allows percentiles only when they cannot point
  to a person. In a large group that is not a problem; in a small subgroup,
  report mean (SD) or leave the row out. See [min, max, median and
  percentiles](export.qmd#min-max-median).

```r
# To Excel: as_hux_xlsx() requires the huxtable package to be INSTALLED
# (you don't need to call library(huxtable) yourself - gtsummary uses it behind the scenes).
table1 %>% as_hux_xlsx(file = "table1.xlsx") # write the table to a .xlsx file

# To Word: requires the flextable package installed
table1 %>%
  as_flex_table() %>% # convert to a flextable object ...
  flextable::save_as_docx(path = "table1.docx") # ... and write it to a .docx file

# Works ALWAYS without extra packages (base R): turn the table into a data frame and save as CSV
table1 %>%
  as_tibble() %>% # the table as a plain data frame
  write.csv("table1.csv", row.names = FALSE) # a CSV opens directly in Excel
```

If `huxtable` or `flextable` is not available on DST, use the CSV route (base R,
no packages needed) or contact your data manager.

## Alternative package

`finalfit::summary_factorlist()` builds a similar baseline table and is popular
in epidemiology. `gtsummary` is used here because exporting to Excel and Word is
straightforward.
